# Cobblemon: Ecological Resonance — Complete Project Archive (Maximum Detail, Pass 3)

**Purpose of this document:** This is meant to be pasted into a new ChatGPT conversation as a full project update, so that ChatGPT has complete context to keep collaborating on Cobblemon: Ecological Resonance (C.E.R.) without anything being lost. It supersedes two earlier, less-complete export attempts made in this same Claude conversation. Where those were condensed or partial, this one goes as far back in the conversation's actual history as is technically recoverable, and includes small thoughts and asides as well as major decisions — both the user's (Wesley's) ideas and the assistant's (Claude's) — rather than only the "clean" final design conclusions.

**What's in here, in order:**

1. **Section A — The earliest recoverable layer.** A compiled summary (not verbatim — this layer was already summarized before this Claude session's own transcript begins, so the original wording is gone) of the earliest design conversations recoverable at all: Field Guide UI mockups, mod baseline comparisons, the Cobblemon Snap discovery, camera-system untangling, Vanilla Backport research, and more. This is the "oldest" material in this archive.
2. **Section B — The full raw verbatim history dump.** Every single user message this Claude session has any record of, in full and in chronological order, exactly as typed/pasted — including the two enormous ChatGPT-transcript pastes in their entirety, the auto-generated compaction summary that bridged an earlier context reset, and every shorter follow-up message. This is the most complete and literal record possible; nothing in it has been filtered, trimmed, or paraphrased.
3. **Section C — Organized verbatim excerpts and the debugging/build narrative.** A hand-organized walk through what happened using the same verbatim material as Section B, but arranged by topic and interleaved with the assistant's explanations of what was built, what broke, and how it was fixed — useful as a more readable narrative companion to the raw dump. Also documents which topics from the original giant pastes could and could NOT be recovered verbatim, and why.
4. **Section D — The current canonical project documentation.** The complete, up-to-date text of every design doc in the C.E.R. project as of 2026-09-22 — the synthesized, "current state of truth" for the modpack's design, independent of how the conversation got here.
5. **Section E — The Claude Code Q&A and this meta-request thread.** A short unrelated tangent (the user asking about Claude Code, the coding tool) plus the history of this document being requested, revised, and requested again in even more detail.

**A note on completeness:** Section B is the ground truth — if anything in Sections A or C seems to summarize or paraphrase, Section B has the actual original words. Two earlier export attempts in this conversation undersold how much detail was needed; this third pass is deliberately maximal rather than curated, per explicit instruction: *"go as far back as u can and be as detailed as u can, include any small thought, big thought, lost thoughts etc. my ideas your idea etc."*

4. Datapacks vs mods philosophy: "use the lowest-complexity layer that cleanly solves the problem, never choose lower layer merely because possible." Datapack uses identified: resource economy (Resin/Affinity Metal recipes), custom progression via advancements, research unlock logic (not the UI itself), Pokémon research tasks, biome affinity distribution, custom loot, recipes, advancements, structures (with caution), NOT worldgen overhauls (prefer established mods). Decision against Terralith/True Survival as base; Tectonic conditional; Cobblemon Additions for inspiration only. Proposal: build a dedicated "E.R. Core" datapack (data/cobblemon_er/ with advancement, recipe, loot_table, function, predicate, tags, worldgen), split into modules only if needed (Progression/Economy/Research/Recipes/World). KubeJS for cross-mod glue Datapacks can't do.

E.R. relevance ratings given per feature group. Recommendation: Vanilla Backport could become "the modern vanilla foundation" layer, Cobblemon the Pokémon foundation, custom systems the E.R. layer.

Pokebelt [Cobblemon] (Fabric-only currently, dedicated trainer-belt Poké Ball storage/equipment, potential progression tiers) and Cobblemon Trainers naming disambiguation: old discontinued CobblemonTrainers (1.20.1, skip) vs modern stack — RCT API + Radical Cobblemon Trainers (1,500+ trainers, series/progression, level caps, Trainer Card, natural spawning) + Run & Bun (advanced trainer AI: move selection, switching, damage prediction, weather/terrain/abilities/hazards) + newer "Cobblemon Trainers" project (singles/doubles/triples, Battle Phone, trainer categories/locks, Showdown import, Mega/Z-Move/Dynamax/Tera support). 8. Core mod list requested and delivered in LOCKED / PROVISIONAL / OPTIONAL tiers. LOCKED: Cobblemon + deps, FTB Quests/Teams/Library, KubeJS, Patchouli, JEI, ModernFix, FerriteCore, ImmediatelyFast, EntityCulling. PROVISIONAL: Create, Actually Additions (Empowerer reinterpreted as "Affinity Infusion"), dedicated research mod (undecided — architecture instead: Advancements=backend state, FTB Quests=progression UI, Patchouli=knowledge, KubeJS=glue), Cobblemon Trainers/Poke Belt/grass encounter mods. 9. Yatters Biospheres reframed at Wesley's request from "dream world" into **Lost/Corrupted Biomes**: ecosystems corrupted long ago and severed from reality into isolated biospheres (quarantine, not creation). Corruption spectrum: Healthy→Tainted→Corrupted→Lost. Restoration choice mechanic proposed: Purify (restore to Overworld) / Stabilize (keep isolated, preserved) / Harness (control corruption deliberately — produces corrupted Pokémon, unusual forms, unique resources, altered evolution, dangerous encounters — ties into Affinity/research). Corruption made bidirectional: Biosphere→Overworld (restoration) AND Overworld→Biosphere (a healthy biome can destabilize, get corrupted, and become quarantined during play — dynamic world-history mechanic). Titans reframed as possible ecosystem anchors: some Titans are why a Lost ecosystem still exists at all; defeating/capturing one destabilizes it and unlocks restoration research. Lore hierarchy: Normal Biomes → Corrupted Biomes → Lost Biomes → Biospheres/Quarantine Zones → Research & Restoration → Reintroduction to Overworld, with "what caused the corruption" flagged as a late-game mystery, not to be explained early.

Advancements framed as "discoveries/milestones," distinct from FTB Quests as "explicit objectives."

Crystalline (amethyst/crystal weapon+block expansion: Divider longsword w/ Amethyst Rain & Shatter Sweep, Crusher, Gravitate; also noted separate "Upgrade Crystalline" expansion project) flagged as potential Affinity/research-crystal-technology tie-in. Golden's Better Enchanting (collectible-enchantment system via Chiseled Bookshelf book collection, unlocks enchantment levels through discovery rather than random table rolls) flagged as a strong research-progression fit. The Block Box (large vanilla-styled building/decor expansion, no worldgen) — optional building flavor. OmniChest (client-side cross-chest item search + in-world pin/beacon to the chest) — flagged as extremely useful storage QoL for a large Cobblemon world.
13. Aero Islands reframed at Wesley's request from "replace Overworld" into a **vertical ecological layer above the existing Overworld+worldgen mods**: ground level = normal Overworld/Cobblemon ecology; cloud layer = transition; Aero Islands = high-altitude Flying/Dragon/Electric/Psychic/Ice ecosystem with its own low/mid/high/extreme-altitude danger and rarity gradient, ruins, and potential Titan encounters; technical caveat that Aero Islands currently replaces world generation outright rather than layering, so genuine layering requires integration work (biome tags/datapacks, Lithostitched dependency) rather than a drop-in install. World architecture settled as three coexisting layers: Aero Islands (the world above), Yatters/Lost Biomes (the worlds that were lost), primary worldgen (the world people live in) — design principle: "don't let worldgen mods replace each other; give each one a physical place, ecological purpose, or narrative reason to exist."

Exposure mod (full in-game photography/film system: camera, film, developing, printing, photograph NBT reportedly containing entity/subject info) evaluated as a third possible "field research camera" layer distinct from both — its value hinges on whether photograph/entity data is exposed to KubeJS/datapacks/FTB Quests, which was flagged as the next thing to verify rather than assumed.

Related/adjacent mods noted (Remote UI Terminal, Proxy) as further "physical machine → logical interface" precedent.

World Remembers: Dear Diary evaluated as the **primary design reference (not just a candidate mod)** for the Field Guide's memory architecture: automatic event-triggered memories (not exhaustive logging) + manual notes + favorites/search/chapters/coordinates, "little travel notes" tone rather than raw achievement pings. Field Guide restructured into four layers: (1) Pokédex = objective species data, (2) Research = player-discovered facts (encounters, behaviors, habitats, evolution witnessed, weather/time correlations), (3) Journal = personal narrative (manual notes, photos, memorable encounters, milestones), (4) World Memory = automatically-generated significant-event log (first encounter/capture/evolution/shiny/legendary/Titan-transformation entries) tying directly into the photography and Titan systems. Modest Magic (Altar+Pedestal replacement for vanilla enchanting; Infusing/Enchanting/Summoning recipe types; datapack-customizable) proposed as potential Research→Application infrastructure, reinterpreting "Summoning" as Pokémon/material synthesis/manifestation rather than literal monster summoning, feeding into the previously-discussed Fusion Crafting(theory)→Synthesis Chamber(practice) pipeline.

Six-item info request issued (MC version, loader+version, exact Cobblemon version, exact CobbleDex version, actual Cobblemon keybind list, and the three command-test results) with an explicit "don't rebuild the pack yet" instruction, since a fresh-instance reproducible failure is valuable diagnostic data.

26. **Major discovery — Cobblemon Snap** identified as substantially more complete than any of the research-system ideas built so far, prompting Wesley to say this is "far more defined than I thought" and matches his original research-system vision closely. Confirmed feature set: photographs scored on distance/framing/behavior-activity/facing/conditions; multi-Pokémon group photos; **5 built-in research levels per species**; tracks forms, poses/activities, biomes, shiny records, best score, total photos; 3D Pokémon presentation + species entry + gallery; datapack-customizable task system (id/title/description/trigger/target/amount/item+CobbleDollar+command rewards, JSON example given); default tasks exportable/editable and live-reloadable via `/snap reload`. This prompted a full re-architecture proposal: **Cobblemon Snap becomes the mechanical backbone of the Research System**, not merely a photography mod, with the following layering — Snap (observation/photography/research-level mechanics) → Field Journal (personal narrative/knowledge layer, explicitly modeled after Dear Diary from #17: "Snapdex = scientific database, Field Journal = personal research notebook") → FTB Quests (larger narrative/non-photography assignments) → KubeJS/datapacks (glue/custom triggers/rewards) → world/exploration mods (create the environments worth researching). Explicitly framed as possibly meaning "we don't need to build a research system from scratch" — the core may already exist and mainly needs configuring/extending rather than inventing.
27. Cobblemon Snap customizability deep-dive: **Tasks are highly customizable** (title/description/trigger/target/amount/item+CobbleDollar+command rewards, full default-task export/edit/live-reload) — confirmed strong. **Task/research "tabs" or categories are NOT confirmed customizable** — Snapdex's page structure (Pokémon entries/Dex view/Gallery view/Tasks page) is not documented as arbitrarily re-categorizable via datapack; flagged explicitly as an open unknown, not assumed impossible. Workaround proposed: treat each Pokémon's own entry as the de facto "research file" with tasks organized conceptually (Habitat Study/Behavioral Study/Social Study/Environmental Study/Rare Observation) rather than needing literal UI tabs. A second, complementary mod discovered — **Cobblemon: Research Tasks** (5–8 hand-authored tasks per Pokémon for all 1,025 species, in-game task editor with add/delete/live-edit/save-load presets in its 2.0 release) — proposed to run alongside Snap rather than replace it, splitting the system into four distinct layers: Snap = field photographic observation, Research Tasks = Pokémon-specific scientific/interactive objectives (catching/battling/fishing/breeding/evolution/items/moves), Field Journal = narrative/lore layer, FTB Quests = adventure/campaign layer ("Travel to the wetlands," "Investigate the strange Pokémon sightings"). Explicit next research task flagged (not yet completed): map out the full set of Snap's trigger types against C.E.R.'s wishlist (biome-specific photo, time-of-day, weather, cross-species pairs, specific-move-in-use, alpha/rare-variant, near-structure) to determine real trigger-system coverage before committing to Snap as the backbone, since the current version's live-reload/export tooling makes this cheap to test.

The real open technical question identified and left unresolved: whether Snap's research system can recognize **arbitrary Cobblemon aspects/forms** (which would mean Shadow/Fractured/Fusion "just work" if implemented as Cobblemon aspects) versus Snap hardcoding shiny-detection specifically (which would require a companion mod/datapack/KubeJS layer to extend it) — flagged as the next thing to investigate before committing to Snap as the full variant-tracking backbone.

Reconfirmed namespace migration (`vanillabackport:`→`minecraft:` for forward/resource-pack compatibility) and per-feature config toggles as reasons the mod is safe to adopt selectively rather than all-or-nothing.
30. Resource-economy micro-ideas locked: (1) Resin/Resin Clumps as an intermediate raw→processed resource pair feeding into whatever resource-generation system C.E.R. settles on (raw Resin Clump → processed Resin → crafting/generation), giving Pale Garden exploration an economic purpose beyond decoration; (2) **Affinity resource (shard/gem, exact form TBD) + Iron/Gold Ingot → Affinity Metal**, with type-specific outputs sketched (Fire Shard+Iron→Fire Affinity Metal, Electric Shard+Iron→Electric Affinity Metal, Water Shard+Iron→Water Affinity Metal) as a way to make the Affinity system part of the tangible resource economy rather than a purely abstract Pokémon-side mechanic. Clarified that Temperate/Cold/Warm are **vanilla/Vanilla-Backport biome-tag categories** (used by the newer farm-animal-variant system), not something the mod invented as a bespoke affinity taxonomy — proposed reusing that same biome-tag infrastructure as the *starting* classification layer for Affinity biome-distribution, then layering C.E.R.-specific affinity-weighting tags on top (e.g. a "Warm" biome might weight Fire high / Ground+Rock medium / Water low), rather than hard-coding affinities to exactly three climate buckets. Flagged as needing verification: whether these tags are exposed as ordinary Minecraft tags (ideal, keeps Affinity from hard-depending on Vanilla Backport) or are VB's own compatibility-layer tags.
31. **New idea inserted by Wesley outside the ChatGPT transcript, not yet discussed with any assistant**: use Cobblemon Routes as the basis for an optional **Nuzlocke-style route-to-route mode**, mirroring however C.E.R.'s existing Nuzlocke-mode mod/system already works, so players can choose either strict route-to-route progression or the game's normal free-roam exploration. **This is a new, unactioned design idea and should be flagged for follow-up / added to the design backlog or unanswered-questions doc, not treated as already resolved.**
32. Vanilla Backport "pot storage" feature explained in detail on follow-up: it is the modern Decorated-Pot-as-small-storage-container feature (place pot → interact → store items → contents persist with the block, pot remains visually a decorated pot rather than becoming a chest), explicitly small-capacity and not a chest replacement; VB's implementation was patched to fix pots losing contents on reload/dimension-change. Proposed C.E.R. flavor use: distributed small-capacity storage in labs/ranches/field stations (e.g. Apricorns/Poké Balls/evolution items/fossils in a research lab; samples/Resin/Affinity materials in a research station; seeds/berries/feed on a ranch) rather than walls of chests — explicitly flagged as needing verification of exact per-pot item capacity/interaction behavior in C.E.R.'s specific 1.21.1/NeoForge setup before treating it as more than decorative QoL.
33. Sweep-suite work (see separate `CER_Sweep_Suite_Source.md` / `CER_Sweep_Suite_FullTaxonomy.md` / `CER_Sweeps_Quick_Reference.md` — already confirmed, already saved, NOT to be rewritten by this pass): ChatGPT's 73-microsweep + 6-meta-process proposal was confirmed by Wesley, fused into 19 named sweeps + composite processes (TriSweep/Final Pre-Release Sweep/Total Cleanse/Targeted Regression Sweep) by Claude using F.R.M. discretion, plus two new Wesley-coined terms: **Archive Diet** (subtractive fluff-trimming of already-compiled archive material, "trim not purge," runs when an archive file gets "thick") as a companion to the renamed **Archive Intake** (the additive "get new discussion into the archive" mode) — together forming the new **Archive Sweep** (sweep #19, a genuinely new category not in ChatGPT's original list, added to fill a real gap), and **Total Cleanse** (all 19 fused sweeps + both Archive Sweep modes, the maximal pack-AND-documentation reset-and-verify, broader than Final Pre-Release Sweep because it also audits the project's own docs/memory).

Field guide ui idea? Okay so maybe like u open the field guide and a digital scroll like page pops up (think like the communication devices from ruby) and its book/ paper thermed with red edges, and on the page are smaller clickable rectangles that look like embossed pages? with eithier black squiggles to rerepsent words or pokemon sprites/silhouettes to represent specific pokemon entries? and u click them and it opens further into a bigger screen containing more detailed info and entries etc (rough description not down to a science yet)

Yeah — I think this is **much closer to the identity of the Field Guide** than making it look like a conventional Minecraft book or a Pokédex clone.

The important part of your idea is that the **first screen feels like an actual field notebook**, while clicking an entry transitions into a much more information-dense interface.

### Rough UI structure

**1. Open Field Guide**

The screen could feel like a digital version of a physical research notebook:

* parchment/paper-colored central page
* distinctive **red outer edges/binding**
* slightly imperfect paper texture
* maybe subtle page shadows
* interface elements designed to look *printed/embossed* rather than like Minecraft buttons
* possibly a little animation when it opens, like a sheet being pulled up/unrolled

The Ruby communication-device inspiration is especially useful because it gives us a justification for the thing being **digital while still having a paper/document aesthetic**.

---

**2. The index page**

Instead of a list like:

> Pokémon
> Biomes
> Research
> Resources

you'd have little **physical-looking page cards** embedded in the document.

Something like:

```text
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                             │
│              FIELD GUIDE                    │
│                                             │
│  ┌─────────────┐       ┌─────────────┐     │
│  │  ~~~~~~~~   │       │   ◇◇◇◇◇     │     │
│  │  ~~~~~~~~   │       │   ◇◇◇◇◇     │     │
│  │  ~~~~~~~~   │       │   ◇◇◇◇◇     │     │
│  │  RESEARCH   │       │  SPECIES    │     │
│  └─────────────┘       └─────────────┘     │
│                                             │
│  ┌─────────────┐       ┌─────────────┐     │
│  │    ░░░      │       │  ~~~~~~~~   │     │
│  │   ░░░░░     │       │  ~~~~~~~~   │     │
│  │    ░░░      │       │  ~~~~~~~~   │     │
│  │   BIOMES    │       │  RESOURCES  │     │
│  └─────────────┘       └─────────────┘     │
│                                             │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

And crucially, **the contents of those cards could change based on what the player has discovered.**

For an undiscovered Pokémon, for example:

**Silhouette**

`████████`

rather than revealing its name.

For discovered information:

**Pokémon sprite + handwritten/printed name**

And for something that hasn't been encountered at all, you could literally have:

> `~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~`

as fake text.

That would make the Guide feel like an actual **researcher's evolving notebook**.

---

### 3. Clicking a "page" zooms into it

This is where I think your idea gets really good.

Rather than opening an entirely separate GUI, the interface could visually **transition deeper into the document**.

For example:

**Field Guide**

→ click **Species**

→ Species index

→ click **Pikachu**

→ Pikachu research page

So you're effectively navigating:

**Document → Section → Entry → Research details**

That gives us a very natural hierarchy.

And the Pokémon page could then become substantially more sophisticated:

```text
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ← SPECIES                         #025       │
│                                               │
│               ⚡ PIKACHU                      │
│                                               │
│                 [SPRITE]                      │
│                                               │
│  HABITAT                                       │
│  ███████████████████░░                         │
│                                               │
│  BEHAVIOR                                      │
│  ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~             │
│  ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~             │
│                                               │
│  RESEARCH                                     │
│  ☑ Encountered                                │
│  ☑ Photographed                               │
│  □ Observed using ...                         │
│  □ Rare behavior documented                   │
│                                               │
│  VARIANTS                                     │
│  [NORMAL] [SHINY] [SHADOW] [FRACTURED]       │
│                                               │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

And **that's where all the systems we've been discussing can converge**.

The Field Guide becomes the player's *master interface for knowledge* rather than simply another Pokédex.

### And I would keep the visual language consistent

I'd establish a few rules early:

**Red edges = Field Guide itself**

**Paper/card = information**

**Embossed tabs = navigation**

**Black scribbles = information not yet deciphered/unlocked**

**Silhouette = unidentified Pokémon**

**Sprite = identified Pokémon**

**Photograph = player's actual observation**

**Handwritten notes = player-generated/discovered information**

**Stamped/marked sections = completed research**

That gives us a visual vocabulary that can communicate progression **without needing giant "UNLOCKED!" messages everywhere.**

---

### One thing I'd add: physical "tabs"

Your little embossed rectangles could also act as **section tabs**, almost like tabs sticking out of a physical research binder.

For example:

`SPECIES | HABITATS | BEHAVIOR | RESOURCES | RESEARCH | NOTES`

Then within Species:

`DEX | VARIANTS | PHOTOS | OBSERVATIONS`

That would make the interface feel much more like a **field research instrument** than an inventory screen.

And it fits extremely well with the idea we were discussing earlier of integrating things like **Snap photography, special variants, research tasks, resources, biome information, etc.**

I think the guiding principle should be:

> **The Field Guide shouldn't feel like a menu pretending to be a book. It should feel like a digital research notebook that happens to function as a menu.**

That's a pretty strong visual/UX direction for the pack.

YES, exactly like that, thats what it looks like in my head good job.YES, exactly like that, thats what it looks like in my head good job.

Haha, **yes!** That means we’ve got the visual language nailed down. 😄

The particularly useful thing about this mockup is that it gives us a concrete **design target** for the actual implementation. We can now treat the Field Guide as:

* 📕 **Red-bound digital field notebook**
* 📄 **Embossed paper/page cards** as the primary navigation
* 🖼️ **Sprites, silhouettes, and player photographs** as visual research evidence
* ✍️ **Handwritten notes** for observations
* 🔒 **Obscured/scribbled information** for undiscovered knowledge
* 🗂️ **Nested pages** rather than traditional Minecraft menu screens
* 🔖 **Side tabs** for major Field Guide sections
* 🔬 **Research progress integrated directly into entries**
* ✨ **Variant tracking** built into the Pokémon's page
* 📸 **Photos/observations** treated as part of the actual research record

And I really like that the mockup **doesn't look overly futuristic**. The technology is there, but the *presentation* is old-school field research. That fits the E.R. concept extremely well.

I think we should preserve this as the **visual north star** for the Field Guide going forward.


Are there any mods similar to this idea or that have mechanism similar to what is described that e can use as a baseline? or if any mods that dont meet those requirements might make a good baseline u can mention those too.

**Yes — and I found one that is almost uncannily close to what we're imagining.** I think we have a much better starting point than I expected.

## 1. [Field Guide](https://modrinth.com/mod/field-guide?utm_source=chatgpt.com) — closest mechanical baseline

This is the first one I'd investigate seriously.

It is literally an exploration/research Field Guide. You discover entities by scanning them, and successful discoveries unlock entries in your personal guide. It supports:

* entities, blocks, and other discoverable things
* hidden entries/categories
* silhouettes/unknown information
* custom descriptions
* player-written notes
* discovery requirements
* rewards/commands when discoveries occur
* datapack-defined categories and contents
* multiplayer-aware per-server progress
* modded entities without requiring individual integrations ([Modrinth][1])

**And here's the really interesting part:** the current 1.21.1 version has a **Pokémon category when Cobblemon is installed and supports variants**. ([Modrinth][2])

Even better, its latest 1.21.1 release added:

> **Journal tab for general notes**

and **Scholar integration for text editing**. ([Modrinth][3])

So this isn't merely conceptually similar. Mechanically, it overlaps with a *huge* portion of what we've been discussing.

### But I wouldn't necessarily use its UI unchanged.

Our generated design is more elaborate:

**Field Guide**
→ category cards
→ species index
→ individual species page
→ research progression
→ variants
→ photographs
→ observations
→ potentially resources/biomes/etc.

Field Guide gives us a lot of the **backend concept** for this, while we'd want our own visual presentation.

---

# 2. [Patchouli](https://modrinth.com/mod/patchouli?utm_source=chatgpt.com) — probably the most important baseline

This is the other big one.

Patchouli is essentially the standard Minecraft **data-driven in-game book framework**. It provides:

* categories
* entries
* nested navigation
* unlock conditions
* bookmarkable entries
* images
* recipes
* custom page types
* templates
* custom visuals/sounds
* localization
* advancement-driven unlocking ([CurseForge][4])

This maps extremely well to the **"click a little embossed page and go deeper into the document"** concept.

For example:

```text
FIELD GUIDE
│
├── SPECIES
│   ├── Pikachu
│   ├── Eevee
│   └── ...
│
├── HABITATS
│   ├── Forest
│   ├── Mountains
│   └── ...
│
├── RESOURCES
│   ├── Resin
│   └── Affinity
│
└── RESEARCH
    ├── Photography
    ├── Behavior
    └── Variants
```

Patchouli already understands that basic hierarchical relationship.

**The major problem:** Patchouli is fundamentally a *documentation/book system*, not a dynamic Pokémon research database.

So I'd treat it as a **technical reference / possible foundation**, rather than assuming it can produce the entire thing out of the box.

---

# 3. [Modonomicon](https://modrinth.com/mod/modonomicon?utm_source=chatgpt.com) — VERY interesting alternative

This one may actually be more interesting than Patchouli for our purposes.

Modonomicon is inspired by both Patchouli and Thaumcraft's Thaumonomicon, and it has:

* data-driven books
* unlock conditions
* nested content
* multiple page types
* images/items/recipes
* extensibility
* **node/connected-entry navigation**
* index-style navigation
* category views ([Modrinth][5])

The **node view** is particularly interesting because it provides a visual progression/navigation system rather than just a traditional book.

![Image](https://images.openai.com/static-rsc-4/tz6K39vS0RVkEhxy3mtAxO1wRNb9tST3mPdZicLxpKH_kluAQaCcRjt5D4YHY_-W7dq3FfEoqA47xhObHbozr4SQlGblkDTMXNvLvhIakW41rnYUFQZk8UKwuyPQnF6Vrozuv1D14cAnsU8hP9940GvLgOiGOxzsbKju_HzyUD1sVmepvihuThIpGRiTkXBO?purpose=fullsize)

![Image](https://images.openai.com/static-rsc-4/qJ5OWngJbnSVc4e0XlxUGTZGISfCJLblCeLKbdacHrFN33e15Lle_16bYGHCbieVorGz-EU9CAJMaGgLgZ727VI5MssOvEFF7NMuqksn7oW_vDvU3U7yR7YjTIstzPtIhF0ymluS3684AR0Ac32O89k4mfW0pXsv1W2VA1kQcfzVJ3z9svnYtkkhHRILAFRU?purpose=fullsize)

![Image](https://images.openai.com/static-rsc-4/UfvY0JCu-kbg0KPaCduAE7sFJxiSYV2rPyZJDr35pmdh2NonuTQmuWhahxj99I3DUEZdwxvEEiS40S0537CFaiwqZwBKh8hN_-hkPeLTsyHfC1bOn4gfYxVSXxtV6kB7e1DLBlFup1jkKHweZtRulohaOFG0j1_sjD1HLa4Py7X-MDFxS8FOopfJgULvfPAM?purpose=fullsize)

That's useful inspiration for our research system.

And importantly, **Modonomicon has 1.21.1 NeoForge releases**, so if that's the loader/version we're building around, it is technically relevant. ([Modrinth][6])

---

# 4. [Field Notes](https://modrinth.com/mod/field-notes?utm_source=chatgpt.com) — small but *very* relevant

This one isn't our Field Guide, but its UI concept is useful.

It automatically records advancements and presents them in a **spread-page journal**, with:

* multiple entries per spread
* page-turning
* search
* filters
* timestamps
* location
* biome
* dimension
* advancement icon
* descriptions ([CurseForge][7])

That's a really good reference for the **"this isn't a Minecraft menu; it's a research journal"** philosophy.

---

# 5. [Scholar](https://modrinth.com/mod/scholar?utm_source=chatgpt.com) — UI inspiration

Scholar isn't a research system.

It's basically a **better book interface**.

But it does something very relevant visually: it replaces Minecraft's vanilla book interface with a redesigned **two-page book presentation**, formatting tools, colored books, improved reading, etc. ([Modrinth][8])

Interestingly, the Field Guide mod actually uses Scholar integration for text editing. ([Modrinth][3])

So Scholar is worth keeping in mind for the **physical-document aesthetic and interaction model**.

---

# 6. [Guide](https://modrinth.com/mod/guide-mod?utm_source=chatgpt.com) — interesting technical inspiration

This one is less directly applicable, but I wouldn't ignore it.

It has:

* customizable themes
* per-book overrides
* custom colors
* visual effects
* sidebar
* search
* favorites
* hot reload
* images
* Markdown
* 3D multiblock previews
* external/direct-from-disk book content ([Modrinth][9])

That's potentially useful if we're eventually building a **heavily customized guide UI** rather than simply accepting the visual limitations of Patchouli.

---

# The really interesting discovery

There is also a **Cobblemon Field Guide** mod specifically for 1.21.1 NeoForge.

[Cobblemon Field Guide](https://modrinth.com/mod/cobblemon-field-guide?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

It provides lookup information for Pokémon including:

* drops
* spawns
* evolutions
* moves
* breeding
* abilities
* fakemon/modpack-modified Pokémon ([Modrinth][10])

It's much more of an **encyclopedia/lookup tool** than our research journal, but it demonstrates that pulling dynamically generated Cobblemon information into a Field Guide interface is already a viable concept.

---

# So I'd break the candidates down like this

| Mod                       | What we steal/investigate                                                          |
| ------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Field Guide**           | ⭐ Discovery + research + hidden entries + notes + variants + Cobblemon integration |
| **Patchouli**             | ⭐ Book architecture + nested entries + unlock conditions + pages                   |
| **Modonomicon**           | ⭐ Research progression + node/index navigation + extensibility                     |
| **Scholar**               | 📕 Physical book/document UI                                                       |
| **Field Notes**           | 📖 Journal presentation + historical observations                                  |
| **Cobblemon Field Guide** | 🔬 Dynamic Pokémon information                                                     |
| **Guide**                 | 🎨 Highly customizable book UI/theming                                             |

## My current thought for E.R.

I **wouldn't immediately try to build the Field Guide from scratch.**

I'd first test **Field Guide + Patchouli/Modonomicon + Scholar** individually and see which parts of our desired system we can actually get for free.

The ideal architecture might end up being something like:

```text
                 ┌───────────────────┐
                 │   FIELD GUIDE     │
                 │   CUSTOM FRONTEND │
                 └─────────┬─────────┘
                           │
          ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
          ▼                ▼                ▼
     Cobblemon         Research          World/
      data             progress          discoveries
          │                │                │
          └────────────────┼────────────────┘
                           ▼
                    FIELD GUIDE ENTRY
                           │
              ┌────────────┼────────────┐
              ▼            ▼            ▼
           Species      Variants      Photos
              │            │            │
              └────────────┼────────────┘
                           ▼
                      Observations
```

**Field Guide looks like the strongest candidate for the actual research mechanics.** Its current feature set is remarkably aligned with what we've been designing, including the new journal tab, variants, Cobblemon category, hidden discoveries, and configurable datapack content. ([Modrinth][3])

Then **Patchouli/Modonomicon are the things I'd study for the actual information architecture**, while **Scholar/Field Notes are primarily visual/UX references**.

And that means there's a very real possibility that **we don't need to invent the entire Field Guide system ourselves** — we may be able to build our E.R. version by extending/adapting an existing research framework and putting our custom visual identity on top of it.

How are data packs different from mods and where do you think we can use them in the pack? where can they replace mods? Dont just replace a mod with a pack because it's possible, follow the same rules as before, if it's more useful, more efficient, more logical, etc etc etc. Which pack would u chose and why, Are there any pack u think we should make ourselves? etc etc etc

Absolutely. And for **our pack specifically**, I think datapacks are going to be more important than I initially gave them credit for.

The key distinction is:

> **A mod adds capability. A datapack configures or populates capabilities that Minecraft/mods already expose.**

A datapack can define or modify things like recipes, loot tables, advancements, functions, tags, structures, dimensions, biomes and other world-generation data. ([Minecraft Wiki][1])

A mod, by contrast, can introduce genuinely new Java-side behavior: new blocks/items/entities, custom GUIs, networking, rendering, APIs, complex persistent systems, new mechanics, etc.

So I **would not** adopt a "datapacks are better because they're lighter" philosophy. I'd use them where they are actually the *more appropriate engineering layer*.

---

# The rule I'd use for E.R.

I'd classify things into four buckets:

### 🟢 Datapack

Use when we're primarily **defining content or rules**.

Examples:

* recipes
* loot
* advancements
* tags
* spawn/progression rules exposed through data
* structures
* worldgen configuration
* simple scripted events
* research unlock conditions
* custom progression
* balancing vanilla/modded resources

### 🔵 Mod

Use when we need **new functionality**.

Examples:

* Field Guide UI
* new blocks/items/entities
* custom machines
* sophisticated research tracking
* camera systems
* new rendering
* new GUIs
* client-side functionality
* APIs/integration
* complex procedural behavior

### 🟣 KubeJS

Use when the game/mod API exposes something we need to manipulate, but building an entire mod for it would be excessive.

This is particularly useful for **pack-specific glue**.

### 🟠 Resource pack

Use when the underlying mechanics already exist and we're changing **presentation**.

Textures, models, sounds, UI assets, etc.

---

# Where I think datapacks fit into E.R.

And this is where I think we can make the pack considerably cleaner.

## 1. Our resource economy — **YES, absolutely**

This is probably one of the strongest uses.

Remember your:

> Resin / Resin Clumps → resin-based resource generation
> Affinity resource + ingot → Affinity Metal

Those shouldn't necessarily require a dedicated mod.

If we're using **existing items/blocks** from Cobblemon or other mods, a datapack can define the recipes and loot relationships.

For example:

```text
Resin
 ↓
Resin Clump
 ↓
processing/crafting
 ↓
Affinity-related resource
```

And:

```text
Affinity Shard + Iron Ingot
             ↓
       Affinity Iron
```

That's exactly the sort of thing I'd want in a datapack.

**Why?**

Because it's *content design*, not a new technological capability.

And if we decide six months later:

> "Electric Affinity Iron is too cheap."

we change one datapack recipe rather than modifying a mod.

---

# 2. Our custom progression — **YES**

This is another major opportunity.

We can make a custom E.R. progression layer using:

* advancements
* recipes
* loot
* functions
* tags
* predicates
* unlock conditions

Minecraft's data system is surprisingly powerful here. 1.21.1 also has data-driven enchantments and the modern item-component system, so the data-driven side of the game has become substantially more capable. ([Minecraft Wiki][2])

For example:

**Early game**

> Survival → basic Pokémon interaction → first research equipment

**Mid game**

> Affinity research → advanced tools → special Pokémon resources

**Late game**

> Legendary research → advanced machinery → dimensional/world exploration

We could have advancements silently track the underlying progression and let other systems react to them.

---

# 3. Research system — **YES, but not entirely**

This is where I'd be careful.

I **wouldn't make the Field Guide itself a datapack.**

The beautiful UI we just designed?

**That's mod territory.**

But the *content and unlock logic* behind that UI could potentially be datapack-driven.

For example:

```text
Field Guide MOD
       │
       ├── UI
       ├── pages
       ├── navigation
       ├── research display
       │
       └── reads research data
                ↑
                │
          E.R. DATAPACK
                │
        ├── discoveries
        ├── requirements
        ├── rewards
        ├── descriptions
        └── progression
```

This is actually a really attractive architecture.

And it's one reason I like the existing **Field Guide** mod we discussed earlier: it already treats a lot of its content as data-driven rather than hardcoding every possible entry.

---

# 4. Pokémon research tasks — **probably**

This could be fantastic.

Imagine:

### Pikachu

**Research Level 0**

> Unknown Pokémon.

↓

**Encounter**

> Species identified.

↓

**Observation**

> Observe Pikachu in its natural habitat.

↓

**Photography**

> Photograph Pikachu.

↓

**Behavior**

> Observe an Electric-type move.

↓

**Variant**

> Document a rare variant.

↓

**Complete**

> Research complete.

A lot of the underlying triggers could be represented through advancements/functions/tags, **provided the relevant Cobblemon events are accessible to the datapack layer**.

The Field Guide mod could then display the results.

That's much better than hardcoding every Pokémon into a custom Java mod.

---

# 5. Biome affinity distribution — **potentially VERY good**

This relates directly to the idea you had earlier:

> Temperate / Cold / Warm → affinity distribution.

We could potentially define things like:

```text
Cold biome
 ├── Ice affinity
 ├── Water affinity
 ├── Psychic affinity
 └── Dragon affinity (rare)

Temperate biome
 ├── Grass
 ├── Normal
 ├── Electric
 └── Bug

Warm biome
 ├── Fire
 ├── Ground
 ├── Rock
 └── Fighting
```

Whether the **actual spawning mechanics** can be cleanly controlled by datapack depends on what Cobblemon exposes and what the specific mechanic needs.

But the *classification tables/tags/data* absolutely make sense as datapack content.

This is also where I'd investigate whether we can leverage the biome tags that already exist rather than inventing our own climate taxonomy.

---

# 6. Custom loot — **YES**

This is probably one of the biggest mod replacements we can make.

Instead of installing a mod just because:

> "I want Pokémon X to drop resource Y."

we can potentially alter loot tables.

For example:

```text
Pokémon / block / structure
          ↓
      loot table
          ↓
  resin / affinity shard /
  research material / etc.
```

There are already datapacks specifically demonstrating this sort of resource/loot manipulation. ([Modrinth][3])

And loot tables are reloadable, unlike some worldgen changes. ([Minecraft Wiki][1])

---

# 7. Recipes — **definitely datapack**

This one is almost a no-brainer.

I would **not install a recipe mod** simply because we need:

> Resin + Iron → Affinity Iron

or:

> Pokémon material + Minecraft item → research equipment

That's exactly what datapacks are good at.

And because we're building a curated modpack, this gives us a nice centralized place for:

**E.R. Recipes**

rather than scattering recipe modifications across several mods.

---

# 8. Advancements — **definitely datapack**

This could become one of our secret weapons.

Instead of using advancements only for:

> "Mine diamond."

we can use them as the underlying **progression database**.

For example:

```text
ER_RESEARCH
│
├── first_pokemon
├── first_photo
├── first_variant
├── first_affinity
├── first_resin
├── first_legendary
└── complete_region
```

Then other systems can respond to those states.

And importantly, advancements are already part of Minecraft's data-pack system. ([Minecraft Wiki][1])

---

# 9. Custom structures — **potentially**

This one is interesting because we've talked about:

* Pokémon villages
* research stations
* ruins
* special landmarks
* rare encounters
* Aero Islands
* exploration locations

Datapacks can define structures and worldgen data. ([Minecraft Wiki][1])

However...

### I would NOT automatically replace a good structure mod with datapacks.

If a mod gives us:

* better structure generation
* sophisticated placement
* configurable spawning
* biome integration
* structure pools
* good compatibility

then we should keep the mod.

The fact that a datapack *can* generate structures isn't enough.

That's exactly the distinction you asked me to make.

---

# 10. World generation — **this is where I'd be cautious**

Datapacks can do a surprising amount of worldgen.

You can define dimensions, biomes, noise settings, terrain generation, etc. ([Minecraft Wiki][4])

But this is an area where I would **strongly prefer established worldgen mods** if they're giving us something sophisticated.

And this is especially relevant to your previous requirement:

> Don't replace normal Overworld generation just to make another worldgen system work.

For example, **Terralith and Tectonic both exist as datapacks**, but I would *not* conclude:

> "They're datapacks, therefore they're better than mods."

Terralith's own documentation specifically warns about compatibility between its datapack and biome-adding datapacks, and notes differences between its mod and datapack versions. ([Modrinth][5])

Tectonic's datapack is actually designed to work alongside certain biome mods, which makes it interesting, but its mod version also has configuration advantages. ([Modrinth][6])

For **our** pack, I'd rather have:

> established worldgen mods + carefully designed compatibility

than:

> 12 giant datapacks fighting over worldgen.

---

# A particularly important point: datapacks can conflict too

This is easy to overlook.

Datapacks aren't magically modular.

Two datapacks can both try to replace:

```text
minecraft:some_loot_table
```

and one can overwrite the other.

Likewise with recipes, worldgen definitions, tags, etc.

Some changes can be reloaded, while worldgen changes generally require restarting/reopening the world. ([Minecraft Wiki][1])

So I **don't want us accumulating 25 random datapacks.**

That would recreate the exact dependency/compatibility mess we're trying to avoid with mods.

---

# What existing datapacks would I actually use?

This is where I'm more conservative.

## Terralith

**Probably not.**

Not because it's bad — it's extremely established — but because **our worldgen philosophy is already more complicated than "install a terrain overhaul."**

We have:

* Cobblemon
* other worldgen
* Aero Islands
* potentially additional biome systems
* our desire to preserve the normal Overworld

So I'd rather build around the worldgen stack we've already selected.

[Terralith on Modrinth](https://modrinth.com/datapack/terralith?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

---

## Tectonic

**Potentially, but only if it fits our final worldgen stack.**

It's much more specifically about terrain shaping, and the project explicitly documents compatibility with biome mods using systems such as Terrablender/Biolith. ([Modrinth][6])

But again, I'd choose based on the *whole worldgen architecture*, not because it's a datapack.

---

## True Survival

**No.**

Interesting datapack, but it's trying to redesign survival as a whole. ([Modrinth][7])

That's exactly the kind of thing I'd avoid because we'd be importing somebody else's progression philosophy into a heavily curated pack.

---

## Cobblemon Additions

**Maybe for inspiration, potentially not as a dependency.**

It demonstrates how far a Cobblemon-oriented datapack can go with structures and world content. ([Modrinth][8])

I'd rather eventually make our own versions of specific things we actually want.

---

# And this is the part I REALLY think we should do:

## Make our own E.R. datapack.

Not one giant "everything datapack."

I'd make a dedicated:

# **Cobblemon E.R. — Core Data**

Something like:

```text
ER-Core/
│
├── pack.mcmeta
│
└── data/
    └── cobblemon_er/
        │
        ├── advancement/
        │
        ├── recipe/
        ├── loot_table/
        ├── function/
        ├── predicate/
        ├── tags/
        │
        └── worldgen/
```

And I'd make it the **official data layer of the pack.**

---

# What goes in it?

### Resource economy

* Resin
* Resin Clumps
* Affinity resources
* Affinity metal recipes
* renewable-resource mechanics

### Progression

* E.R. progression milestones
* research milestones
* exploration milestones
* special Pokémon discoveries

### Loot

* Pokémon-related drops
* special resource drops
* exploration rewards
* structure rewards

### Recipes

* all E.R.-specific recipes
* recipe balancing
* controlled conversions
* progression-gated recipes where appropriate

### Research hooks

* research advancements
* discovery conditions
* special encounters
* variant discovery
* photography milestones

### World rules

Only things that genuinely belong here.

---

# And I'd potentially split it into modules

This is even better.

```text
ER Core
│
├── ER Core — Progression
├── ER Core — Economy
├── ER Core — Research
├── ER Core — Recipes
└── ER Core — World
```

**But only if we actually need that separation.**

Initially, I'd probably keep it as **one pack with clean internal namespaces/files** rather than creating five separate datapacks.

That gives us one authoritative source of truth.

---

# Where I'd use KubeJS instead

This is important because otherwise we'd end up forcing datapacks to do things they're bad at.

For example:

> "When this Cobblemon Pokémon performs this specific action, modify this other mod's machine behavior."

If Cobblemon exposes an event that KubeJS can hook into but datapacks can't, that's a **KubeJS job**.

Likewise complicated recipe scripting involving several mods may be cleaner in KubeJS.

So I'd envision:

```text
             E.R. PACK
                 │
       ┌─────────┼─────────┐
       │         │         │
       ▼         ▼         ▼
   DATAPACK    KUBEJS    MODS
       │         │         │
   content     glue     capability
   + rules     logic    + systems
```

That separation is **much cleaner** than trying to make one technology do everything.

---

# And there's one more really useful thing

Because we're on **1.21.1**, datapack version 48 is the relevant format for that version. Mojang's 1.21 changes also renamed many datapack directories from plural to singular, such as `recipes → recipe`, `functions → function`, and `loot_tables → loot_table`. ([Minecraft Feedback][9])

So when we start making our own pack, we should build it **specifically for our target Minecraft version** rather than grabbing old datapack tutorials and assuming the structure is still correct.

---

# My current E.R. philosophy

I'd actually write this down as one of our pack-development rules:

> **Use the lowest-level tool that cleanly solves the problem, but never choose a lower-level tool merely because it is possible.**

So:

**"Change a recipe?"**
→ Datapack.

**"Change loot?"**
→ Datapack.

**"Create research progression?"**
→ Datapack where possible.

**"Create the Field Guide interface?"**
→ Mod/framework.

**"Need complex cross-mod scripting?"**
→ KubeJS.

**"Need a genuinely new gameplay mechanic?"**
→ Mod.

**"Need new art?"**
→ Resource pack.

**"Need giant worldgen overhaul?"**
→ Whichever established worldgen system fits our architecture — mod or datapack — not automatically datapack.

And I think **our own E.R. Core datapack is absolutely worth making**. It could eventually become the glue that makes the entire pack feel like **one designed game rather than a collection of mods**.

That, more than simply replacing mods, is where I think datapacks could become really valuable for this project.

Research and analyze the vanilla backport mod and make a list of featurres it would add if we included it in the pack

Yes. I checked the **current 1.21.1 NeoForge release line** of Vanilla Backport rather than treating it as the older “Caves & Cliffs backport” people may remember. The current project has grown into a fairly large collection of vanilla update backports, and **1.21.1-1.1.7.10** is the current 1.21.1 release listed by CurseForge as of June 11, 2026. ([CurseForge][1])

For our Cobblemon E.R. pack, there is actually **a lot here**.

## Vanilla Backport — what it would add to our pack

The current 1.21.1 version covers:

* **Caves & Cliffs**
* **The Wild Update**
* **The Garden Awakens**
* **Spring to Life**
* **Bundles of Bravery**
* **Armored Paws**
* **Bats & Pots**
* **Chase the Skies**
* **Chaos Cubed**

The developer describes the project's scope as primarily **content**—blocks, entities, world generation, etc.—rather than trying to backport every underlying technical/data-system change. Most individual content features are configurable. ([GitHub][2])

---

# 1. Caves & Cliffs content

This is the older 1.16.5 backport portion.

### Blocks/resources

* Copper
* Copper ore
* Raw copper
* Copper blocks
* Waxed copper
* Lightning rods
* Amethyst
* Amethyst geodes
* Tuff
* Smooth basalt
* Deepslate
* Glow lichen
* Moss
* Azalea
* Flowering azalea
* Hanging roots
* Rooted dirt
* Dripstone
* Pointed dripstone
* Small dripleaf
* Big dripleaf
* Spore blossoms
* Glow berries

The backport also implements things like copper stonecutting recipes, waxing/unwaxing behavior, waterlogging for relevant blocks, and dripstone growth. ([CurseForge][3])

### Mobs

* **Goats**
* **Glow Squids**

Goats include their mountain spawning, jumping, ramming, breeding and behavioral mechanics. Glow squids can spawn in underground water. ([CurseForge][4])

### World generation

* Lush Cave-style cave biomes
* Dripstone cave content
* Amethyst geodes
* Deepslate generation
* Tuff
* Underground glow-lichen/moss features
* Noise cave generation
* Cave biome API integration

The mod's old Caves & Cliffs implementation actually contains its own cave-generation infrastructure, including smaller noise caves and support for other cave-biome mods. ([CurseForge][3])

### Why this matters for E.R.

This gives us a much more **modern vanilla underground** underneath all of the Cobblemon content.

And importantly, it gives us a bunch of materials that can potentially interact with our eventual:

* Affinity system
* research system
* machines
* crafting progression
* Pokémon synthesis
* exploration progression

---

# 2. The Wild Update

The 1.18.2 portion brings the major Wild Update content forward. Vanilla Backport's current roadmap explicitly lists **The Wild Update** as one of its completed legacy backports. ([GitHub][2])

That means:

### Deep Dark

* Deep Dark biome
* Ancient Cities
* Sculk
* Sculk Veins
* Sculk Catalyst
* Sculk Sensor
* Reinforced/deep-dark related structures/content
* Warden

### Mangrove

* Mangrove Swamp
* Mangrove trees
* Mangrove wood set
* Mangrove roots
* Mud
* Mud bricks
* Muddy mangrove roots
* Propagules
* Mangrove-related vegetation

### Mobs

* **Warden**
* **Allay**
* **Frog**
* **Tadpole**

### Other

* Goat horn-related content
* Froglights
* Recovery compass
* Echo shards
* Swift Sneak
* Mud mechanics
* Boat with chest
* Ancient City loot

For this pack specifically, **the Warden + Ancient City + Deep Dark** is probably the most interesting part.

It gives us an actual vanilla endgame-adjacent danger zone that can coexist with our Pokémon progression rather than everything being "Cobblemon overworld exploration."

---

# 3. The Garden Awakens

This is a *huge* one for atmosphere.

Vanilla Backport adds the complete core Garden Awakens package, including:

### Pale Garden

* **Pale Garden biome**
* Pale Oak
* Pale Oak logs
* Pale Oak planks
* Pale Oak leaves
* Pale Oak saplings
* Pale hanging moss
* Pale moss
* Pale moss carpet
* Pale vegetation
* Pale garden generation

### Eyeblossoms

* Closed Eyeblossom
* Open Eyeblossom
* Eyeblossom behavior
* Emissive appearance

### Resin

* Resin blocks
* Resin clumps
* Resin bricks
* Resin-related generation
* Resin armor trim material

### Creaking

* **Creaking mob**
* **Creaking Heart**
* Creaking behavior
* Creaking spawning in Pale Gardens

The original Garden Awakens backport specifically lists the Creaking Heart, Pale Oak woodset, pale moss variants, eyeblossoms, resin materials, Creaking and Pale Garden. ([Modrinth][5])

It also has advancements such as **Heart Transplanter**, for correctly placing a Creaking Heart, in the current 1.21.1 implementation. ([Modrinth][6])

### E.R. relevance

**Extremely high.**

The Pale Garden is almost tailor-made for the kind of weird Minecraft/Pokémon hybrid atmosphere we're building.

It could become:

* a rare research biome
* an Affinity-related biome
* a place associated with unusual Pokémon
* a location for a Titan encounter
* a spooky late-game exploration zone

---

# 4. Spring to Life

This one is less mechanically significant but **massively improves the vanilla world**.

Vanilla Backport adds:

### World ambience

* Leaf litter
* Wildflowers
* Bushes
* Firefly bushes
* Falling leaves
* Fallen trees
* Dry grass
* Tall dry grass
* Desert ambient sounds
* Firefly ambience

The current implementation specifically makes falling leaves configurable and client-side. ([Modrinth][7])

### New animal variants

Cows, pigs and chickens get:

* Temperate variants
* Cold variants
* Warm variants

Chicken variants also get corresponding colored eggs:

* Blue eggs
* Brown eggs

The variants are determined by the biome rather than being completely separate mob species. ([Modrinth][7])

### Other

* Updated camel spawning
* Sheep spawning/color priorities
* Cactus flowers
* Additional vegetation
* Various vanilla recipe/UI updates

---

# 5. Wolf variants

This deserves its own section because **Cobblemon players are going to notice it immediately.**

Vanilla Backport adds the modern wolf variants:

* Pale
* Spotted
* Snowy
* Black
* Ashen
* Rusty
* Woods
* Chestnut
* Striped

They can be assigned based on biome tags. ([Modrinth][7])

It also adds modern **wolf sound personalities**, including:

* Classic
* Puglin
* Sad
* Angry
* Grumpy
* Big
* Cute

Those are independently configurable/data-driven as well. ([Modrinth][7])

That's a nice example of something that isn't technically "important" but makes the Minecraft side of the pack feel much newer.

---

# 6. Armored Paws

This brings in the modern armadillo content.

### Armadillo

* **Armadillos**
* Armadillo spawning
* Armadillo behavior
* Armadillo scutes
* Wolf armor
* Spider fear response

The current backport specifically adds armadillos and makes their spawning configurable. Spiders can become afraid of them, matching modern vanilla behavior. ([Modrinth][7])

---

# 7. Bats & Pots

Two particularly nice little additions:

### Bats

* Updated bat model/appearance
* Modern bat behavior/visuals

### Decorative pots

Decorated pots can **store items**.

That's surprisingly useful for a modpack because it turns decorated pots from purely decorative blocks into another storage/decor system. ([Modrinth][7])

---

# 8. Bundles of Bravery

This is one of the more mechanically useful additions.

### Bundles

* Modern bundle behavior
* Updated Bundle UI
* Updated bundle controls
* Dyable bundles
* Modern bundle models
* Legacy/modern bundle modes

The implementation even allows the bundle behavior/model to be switched between legacy and modern versions. ([Modrinth][7])

### E.R. relevance

Pretty good.

With Cobblemon, exploration gets inventory-heavy **fast**.

Bundles are particularly useful for:

* catching supplies
* apricorns
* berries
* fossils/materials
* research materials
* Affinity components
* miscellaneous loot

---

# 9. Chase the Skies

This is probably the **biggest individual addition** for our pack.

## Dried Ghast

* Dried Ghast block
* Dried Ghast generation/acquisition
* Hydration mechanics
* Piglin bartering acquisition

The current implementation even has an advancement for putting a Dried Ghast into water. ([Modrinth][6])

## Happy Ghast

**Happy Ghast**

with:

* Growth stages
* Riding
* Harness
* Multiplayer riding
* Flying
* Leashing
* Harness textures
* Updated movement behavior

The mod also supports custom harnesses through its compatibility system and recognizes items tagged as harnesses. ([Modrinth][6])

### E.R. implications

This is **very significant**.

A Happy Ghast gives us a legitimate vanilla flying transport option without introducing a giant tech/modded aircraft system.

That could make exploration of our custom Pokémon world feel dramatically different.

---

# 10. Tears music disc

The Ghast update also adds:

**Tears music disc**

Obtained by killing a Ghast by deflecting a fireball/fire charge back at it. ([Modrinth][8])

Small feature, but nice for collection/progression.

---

# 11. Chaos Cubed

This is the newest major addition in the current 1.21.1 release.

And **this is the part I would pay particular attention to for E.R.**

Vanilla Backport 1.1.7 adds:

### Sulfur Caves

A new biome:

**Sulfur Caves**

### New blocks

#### Cinnabar

* Cinnabar
* Polished Cinnabar
* Cinnabar Bricks
* Chiseled Cinnabar

#### Sulfur

* Sulfur
* Polished Sulfur
* Sulfur Bricks
* Chiseled Sulfur

### Other sulfur content

* Potent Sulfur
* Sulfur Spikes
* Sulfur Springs
* Sulfur Cubes
* Bucket of Sulfur Cubes
* Sulfur Cube archetypes

It also adds a new **"Uh Oh"** Husbandry advancement involving a Sulfur Cube absorbing TNT. ([CurseForge][9])

---

# 12. Sulfur Cube variants

This is where Chaos Cubed starts getting particularly interesting.

The Sulfur Cube has different **archetypes**, which essentially give it different behavior.

That includes things such as:

* bouncing behavior
* explosive behavior
* other specialized cube behaviors

The current release has configuration options for the Chaos Cubed systems as well. ([CurseForge][9])

And Vanilla Backport has already been updating things like Sulfur Cube persistence, buoyancy, explosion behavior, etc. in subsequent 1.1.7.x releases. ([CurseForge][10])

---

# 13. Chaos Cubed technical infrastructure

This is important even though players won't necessarily see it.

Vanilla Backport also adds infrastructure required for the Chaos Cubed content:

### New attributes

* Bounciness
* Air drag modifier
* Friction modifier

### Worldgen infrastructure

* New surface rules
* Spatial noise threshold
* Noise threshold
* Trapezoid IntProvider
* Weighted random selector
* Sequence feature
* Template feature

And it changes knockback resistance to support a minimum value of `-2.0`. ([CurseForge][9])

This means Vanilla Backport isn't merely adding decorative blocks; some of its systems are sufficiently deep to support the modern mechanics.

---

# 14. Modern vanilla ambience

There's actually a surprisingly large amount of **"Minecraft feels newer"** content.

Examples:

* Falling leaves
* Falling conifer needles
* Firefly bushes
* Fireflies
* New ambient desert sounds
* Pale Garden ambience
* Eyeblossom emissive behavior
* Updated mob sounds
* New animal variants
* Updated animations
* New background music

The current Bundle o' Life update alone adds five Amos Roddy background tracks, including *Fireflies* and *Lilypad*. ([Modrinth][7])

---

# 15. Vanilla creative/inventory integration

Vanilla Backport doesn't just dump everything into some giant modded creative tab.

It has a **bundled creative-tab system** that lets you switch between the contents of different backported updates through a vertical menu. ([Modrinth][7])

It also supports conventional tags used by things like:

* Forge
* Fabric
* Create

That is useful for a pack as heavily integrated as ours. ([Modrinth][7])

---

# 16. Data/resource-pack compatibility

This is probably one of the more important things for **our development process**.

The modern version migrated its features from the old:

`vanillabackport`

namespace into:

`minecraft`

This was specifically done to improve forward compatibility with vanilla versions and resource packs. ([Modrinth][7])

It also supports data-driven variants, including:

* wolf variants
* farm animal variants
* wolf sound variants
* biome tags
* structure conditions
* moon-phase conditions

That means we could potentially use some of this infrastructure when creating custom content around the pack.

---

# 17. Configurability

This is arguably one of the biggest reasons I'd consider including it.

The developer explicitly says the project tries to make **most individual features configurable** rather than forcing the entire backport on you. ([Modrinth][11])

Examples from the current release include toggles/configuration for:

* Leaf litter
* Wildflowers
* Bushes
* Firefly bushes
* Dry grass
* Fallen trees
* Falling leaves
* Farm animal variants
* Wolf variants
* Armadillos
* Camel spawning
* Creaking-related behavior
* Happy Ghast movement
* Music
* Villager/wandering trader trades
* Dried Ghast acquisition
* Resin generation
* Music-disc drops
* Pale Garden effects
* Chaos Cubed features

So we wouldn't necessarily have to accept every single piece of it.

---

# What this means for **our** pack

I'd break the value down differently than a normal modpack.

| Feature group               | E.R. value |
| --------------------------- | ---------- |
| Caves & Cliffs              | ⭐⭐⭐⭐       |
| Wild Update                 | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐      |
| Garden Awakens              | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐      |
| Spring to Life              | ⭐⭐⭐⭐       |
| Armored Paws                | ⭐⭐⭐        |
| Bats & Pots                 | ⭐⭐⭐        |
| Bundles                     | ⭐⭐⭐⭐       |
| Chase the Skies             | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐      |
| Chaos Cubed                 | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐      |
| Ambient/visual improvements | ⭐⭐⭐⭐       |
| Configurability             | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐      |

### The REALLY interesting pieces for E.R.

I'd specifically flag:

**Warden + Ancient Cities**
→ natural high-level exploration challenge.

**Pale Garden + Creaking**
→ extremely compatible with the eerie/mysterious side of our world.

**Happy Ghast**
→ vanilla aerial transportation without needing another major transportation system.

**Sulfur Caves + Chaos Cubed**
→ potentially an entire specialized underground environment that could interact with our Affinity/technology progression.

**Modern animal variants**
→ makes the Minecraft ecosystem feel much more alive alongside Cobblemon.

**Bundles**
→ legitimately useful for Pokémon exploration.

**Modern world generation/ambience**
→ makes the base world feel closer to modern Minecraft despite us being on 1.21.1.

---

## One VERY important caveat

I **wouldn't treat Vanilla Backport as "free modern Minecraft."**

The author explicitly says the project prioritizes **content backports**, not complete technical backports. So things such as modern underlying data-component architecture aren't necessarily coming along with it. ([Modrinth][11])

And because our pack is already extremely complicated—Cobblemon + NeoForge + Sinytra/cross-loader stuff + tech mods + custom E.R. systems—I would test it against the actual finalized mod list rather than assuming compatibility.

But from a **design standpoint**, Vanilla Backport fits our project unusually well.

In fact, there's an interesting consequence:

> **Vanilla Backport could effectively become the "modern vanilla foundation" of E.R., while Cobblemon becomes the Pokémon foundation and our custom systems become the E.R. layer.**

That gives us a much more coherent base than adding dozens of individual "vanilla+ feature" mods.

And notably, the current project is still actively being developed; **1.21.1 NeoForge 1.1.7.10** is available, with the project also having a roadmap for additional modern updates such as Copper Age and Mounts of Mayhem. ([CurseForge][10])

poke belt and cat. (cobblemon trainers) look into these two mods


I looked into both. There’s a naming wrinkle with **“CAT / Cobblemon Trainers”**, so I want to distinguish what I found rather than accidentally analyze the wrong project.

## 1. Pokebelt [Cobblemon]

[Pokebelt [Cobblemon] on Modrinth](https://modrinth.com/mod/pokebelt-cobblemon?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

This is a **1.21.1 Fabric** Cobblemon QoL mod. It adds an actual trainer-style belt that provides dedicated Poké Ball storage. It is client + server and is MIT licensed. ([Modrinth][1])

### What it actually does

The core idea is:

> **Move Poké Balls out of the normal inventory and into a dedicated trainer equipment/storage system.**

It supports:

* Poké Balls
* Great Balls
* Ultra Balls
* custom Cobblemon balls
* dedicated belt storage
* upgradeable storage
* trainer-themed visual equipment

So rather than giving the player another generic backpack, it specifically makes the **Pokémon trainer's belt an actual gameplay object**. ([Modrinth][1])

### Why I think this is interesting for E.R.

This is **much more relevant to our design than it initially sounds**.

We've been discussing the trainer as an actual game-system entity rather than just "Minecraft player + Pokémon."

A Pokébelt gives us a natural physical representation of:

**Trainer → Poké Ball equipment → Pokémon party**

And it could potentially become part of the progression system.

For example:

**Basic Belt**
→ 3–4 ball slots

**Trainer Belt**
→ 6 ball slots

**Advanced Belt**
→ additional storage

**Specialized belt**
→ Quick Ball / Dusk Ball / Luxury Ball organization, etc.

However, I would **not immediately add it** to our pack.

The big problem is that our planned **6-Pokémon selection wheel** already provides a dedicated interaction layer. We need to determine whether Pokebelt is merely inventory storage or whether we could make it coexist with the actual active-party UI without creating redundant systems.

Also, the currently listed version is **Fabric only**, which matters because our target foundation is NeoForge. ([Modrinth][1])

So I'd currently categorize it as:

**Cool concept → potentially useful → compatibility problem → investigate before adopting.**

---

# 2. "Cobblemon Trainers"

There are actually **several different projects with extremely similar names**, which is probably where the CAT reference is coming from.

The important ones I found are:

### Original CobblemonTrainers

[CobblemonTrainers on CurseForge](https://www.curseforge.com/minecraft/mc-mods/cobblemontrainers?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

This is the original project by selfdot.

It is **discontinued** and was for **1.20.1**, Forge/Fabric. ([CurseForge][2])

Its big feature was customizable trainer battles.

You could create trainers and specify:

* Pokémon
* levels
* IVs
* EVs
* abilities
* moves
* natures
* trainer groups
* cooldowns
* level restrictions
* win commands
* loss commands
* defeat requirements
* whether a trainer can only be beaten once

It also had Generation 5-inspired AI and support for trainer entities. ([CurseForge][2])

**We should not use this version.**

It's effectively historical at this point.

---

# 3. The important modern successor: Radical Cobblemon Trainers

[Radical Cobblemon Trainers](https://modrinth.com/mod/rctmod?loader=neoforge&version=1.21.1&utm_source=chatgpt.com)

This one is **very relevant to our pack**.

It currently supports:

* **Minecraft 1.21.1**
* **NeoForge**
* Fabric
* Forge
* Cobblemon
* its own RCT API

and was updated **September 7, 2026**. ([CurseForge][3])

It contains **1,500+ trainers** from Radical Red, Unbound, BDSP, etc., with natural spawning, progression and trainer-card functionality. ([CurseForge][3])

### But here's the important part for E.R.

RCT isn't merely a "spawn some NPCs and fight them" mod.

It has:

### Trainer progression

Trainers can be organized into series.

The player progresses through trainers, with key trainers acting as progression gates. ([Modrinth][4])

### Level caps

RCT can prevent Pokémon above the current progression cap from gaining XP until the relevant trainer/key trainer has been defeated. ([Modrinth][4])

### Trainer Card

Players get an actual Trainer Card that tracks:

* progression
* defeated trainers
* upcoming key trainers
* series
* level cap progression

([Modrinth][4])

### Natural trainers

Trainers actually appear in the world according to biome/spawning rules.

That makes them feel considerably more like **Pokémon-world NPCs** than commands/GUIs.

---

# 4. And then there's Run & Bun

This is where things get particularly interesting.

[Cobblemon: Run & Bun (Advanced Trainer AI)](https://modrinth.com/mod/cobblemon-recobbled-%28advanced-trainer-ai%29/versions?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

Run & Bun is an advanced trainer-AI system built around RCT.

It supports:

* move selection
* switching
* damage prediction
* status considerations
* weather
* terrain
* abilities
* hazards
* more sophisticated decision making

and currently supports **1.21.1 Fabric and NeoForge**. ([Modrinth][5])

This is particularly relevant because the RCT ecosystem's API explicitly supports:

* singles
* doubles
* multi battles
* custom battle rules
* Mega Evolution
* Dynamax
* Z-Moves
* Terastallization
* trainer-held items

depending on the relevant mods. ([CurseForge][6])

---

# 5. There's also a newer "Cobblemon Trainers" project

I found another project literally called:

**Cobblemon Trainers**

[Cobblemon Trainers on Modrinth](https://modrinth.com/mod/cobblemon-trainers-rerebleue?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

This one is **1.21.1 Fabric**, recently updated, and is conceptually very interesting.

Rather than automatically filling the world with trainers, it deliberately makes trainers **placed/called content**. ([Modrinth][7])

It supports:

* singles
* doubles
* triples
* battle music
* Battle Phone
* trainer progression
* trainer categories
* trainer locks
* advancements
* custom trainer skins
* custom Pokémon
* regional forms
* fakemon
* Showdown team import
* configurable AI
* one-time trainers
* rewards
* dialogue
* custom trainer packs

And notably:

### It supports battle gimmicks

Trainers can use:

* Mega Evolution
* Z-Moves
* Dynamax
* Terastalization

with the appropriate dependencies. ([Modrinth][7])

That is a **very attractive architecture for what we're building**.

---

# So which one did you mean by "CAT"?

If by **CAT** you meant the old **CobblemonTrainers** project, that's essentially obsolete for our 1.21.1 NeoForge pack.

If you meant the **current Cobblemon trainer ecosystem**, then the important stack is:

**RCT API**
↓
**Radical Cobblemon Trainers**
↓
**Run & Bun**
↓
optional trainer/badge/datapack content

That stack is actually something I'd seriously consider for E.R.

---

# And there's a BIG design implication for our pack

I don't think we should think about trainers as merely:

> "NPCs that initiate Pokémon battles."

We could make them one of the **major progression layers of E.R.**

Something like:

**World exploration**
→ encounter trainer
→ trainer battle
→ earn rewards
→ unlock research/progression
→ increase trainer level cap
→ access stronger areas/trainers
→ eventually challenge major bosses/Titans/etc.

That would mesh extremely well with our existing ideas around **research, Affinity, Titans and progression**.

And RCT already provides several pieces we'd otherwise have to build ourselves.

### My current assessment

| Mod/system                     | E.R. relevance | Problem                                                |
| ------------------------------ | -------------: | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Pokebelt**                   |           ⭐⭐⭐⭐ | Fabric-only currently                                  |
| Original CobblemonTrainers     |             ⭐⭐ | Discontinued / 1.20.1                                  |
| **Radical Cobblemon Trainers** |          ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ | Need to integrate its progression philosophy with ours |
| **RCT API**                    |          ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ | Excellent underlying trainer infrastructure            |
| **Run & Bun**                  |          ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ | AI may be extremely useful                             |
| New Cobblemon Trainers         |           ⭐⭐⭐⭐ | Fabric-only currently, but architecture is interesting |

**The RCT + Run & Bun combination is the one I'd investigate much more deeply for our pack.**

And I would **not add RCT blindly** yet. We should first map out exactly what we want *our* trainer system to do—especially how trainers, gyms, research, Affinity, Titans, level caps and our eventual Pokémon selection wheel interact—then see which pieces RCT can supply instead of reinventing them.

grassier grass mod and the one pokemon mod that makes walking in grass start encounters?

Yep — I think you’re remembering **two separate things**, and they actually fit the pack really well.

### 🌿 Grassier Grass

Grassier Grass makes Minecraft's normally flat grass look like **actual dense, swaying grass**. It's client-side and has a 1.21.1 NeoForge version. ([Modrinth][1])

That could be especially good for our pack because it makes designated encounter areas *visually* read as Pokémon-style tall grass rather than just "Minecraft happened to have some grass here."

### ⚔️ The Pokémon encounter one

I found **Cobblemon Wild Spawn** — this is almost certainly the one you're thinking of.

Cobblemon Wild Spawn

It specifically makes walking through grass trigger Pokémon encounters, with the Pokémon being selected using **Cobblemon's normal spawn data**, so biome, conditions, rarity, etc. still matter. It can also automatically start the battle when the encounter occurs. ([CurseForge][2])

And importantly for our pack:

* **Minecraft 1.21.1**
* **NeoForge support**
* Grass encounters
* Water encounters
* Automatic battle initiation
* Uses Cobblemon's existing spawn data
* Configurable encounter chances/cooldowns
* Repels
* Lures
* Type Lures
* Shiny-rate configuration
* Can even disable Cobblemon's normal natural spawning if desired ([Modrinth][3])

There's also an older **WildEncounters [Cobblemon]** datapack that does the simpler version: walk into tall grass → chance of a Pokémon appearing. ([Modrinth][4])

### For *our* pack

I'd put **Cobblemon Wild Spawn** on the shortlist over the datapack.

The really interesting possibility is:

**Grassier Grass + Cobblemon Wild Spawn + our encounter/battle systems**

→ visually obvious Pokémon grass
→ walking into it can trigger an encounter
→ encounter immediately launches the battle
→ Pokémon selection wheel appears if appropriate
→ no awkward "Pokémon spawned and is just standing there" phase.

That would give us a much more **Pokémon-native overworld encounter loop** while still letting Cobblemon handle the actual Pokémon spawn tables. ([Modrinth][3])

And I especially like it because we could potentially use **Grassier Grass as the visual layer** and **Cobblemon Wild Spawn as the mechanical layer**, rather than trying to make a giant custom encounter system ourselves.
